turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Hi. Well, I'm here because I just can't seem to shake this feeling that work isn't safe anymore. And... I don't know, I just feel like I'm somehow damaged now. Like the competent person who got promoted just isn't really there anymore.

turns.doctor_question: Can you tell me more about this feeling that work isn't safe anymore?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I just... I try to avoid being there in certain situations now. I have some flexibility, so I've started trading shifts with coworkers, or pushing back on our release windows. I just work from home whenever I possibly can. 

And if I do have to actually go into the office, I always take the side entrance now. I just can't... I mean, walking through that main lobby after dark just makes me feel like I’m going to completely come apart.

symptom_reasoning.S070: The patient describes active external avoidance of workplace-related reminders of the trauma, including trading shifts, working from home, and taking the side entrance to avoid the main lobby.

turns.doctor_question: Did something specific happen at work that made you start feeling this way?

turns.doctor_question: Are there any other places or situations, outside of work, that you avoid because they make you feel anxious or uncomfortable?

No, not really. I mean... I think it's mostly just tied to work. Outside of that, I don't really avoid anywhere else. I still go out to run errands or see friends and I feel okay. 

It's really just the office, or I guess being alone in a big commercial building at night. But in my normal, personal life... no, I haven't noticed anything like that.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever find yourself reliving the break-in at the building in your mind?

Yeah, I do. It doesn't take much to set it off, honestly. Just hearing a badge scanner beep, or... heavy footsteps out in the hallway. Even just getting a late-night deployment alert on my phone can do it. 

When that happens, it just suddenly puts me right back in that office. My chest gets completely tight, and I just see the image of the guard on the floor... it just cuts right through whatever I’m trying to do in that moment.

symptom_reasoning.S069: The patient confirms reliving the traumatic break-in triggered by specific cues, describing intrusive memories, feeling pulled back into the event, and experiencing physiological distress such as chest tightness.

turns.doctor_question: Do you try to avoid thinking or talking about the break-in at your office?

Yeah, I do. I try not to talk about it or even think about it if I can help it. It's actually gotten to the point where I avoid anything that brings it up... I’ve started trading shifts and pushing back on my release windows just so I don't have to be in those situations. 

I just work from home whenever I can now. And if I absolutely have to go into the office, I take the side entrance... because just walking through that main lobby after dark makes me feel like I’m going to come apart. So, yeah, I basically do whatever I can to avoid dealing with it.

symptom_reasoning.S070: The patient explicitly confirms avoiding thinking and talking about the break-in, as well as engaging in extensive external avoidance behaviors such as trading shifts, working from home, and using a side entrance to avoid the lobby.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find yourself being easily startled by small things?

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel guilty about what happened during the break-in at your office?

symptom_reasoning.S073: The patient explicitly confirms experiencing distorted cognitions and self-blame regarding the traumatic break-in, believing they could have prevented the guard from being hurt despite knowing they were terrified and hiding.
